property_summary: For every call to fallback with any msg.value, the reference contract only accepts exactly 10 ether and therefore after a successful call pastBlockTime is strictly greater than the previous value; the mutant allowing msg.value >= 10 ether can accept larger payments which lets calls with value >10 ether succeed and thus can advance pastBlockTime when the reference would have reverted.

For any call to fallback with any msg.value, the reference contract only accepts calls when msg.value == 10 ether and then advances pastBlockTime (so after a successful call block.timestamp > previous pastBlockTime), whereas the mutant accepting msg.value >= 10 ether can succeed on values >10 ether when the reference would revert, causing pastBlockTime to advance in cases the reference would not — so the rule: "If a fallback call with msg.value != 10 ether is accepted by c, then msg.value must equal 10 ether" (i.e. the reference never accepts values ≠10 ether, the mutant sometimes does).

Reference C only accepts fallback calls that send exactly 10 ether (calls with other msg.value revert); the mutant accepts msg.value >= 10 ether so some calls with msg.value != 10 ether that the reference rejects will succeed in the mutant, leading to different post-call pastBlockTime behavior.

For any caller sending exactly 10 ether to C.fallback, the reference contract only updates pastBlockTime when block.timestamp strictly increases (so if block.timestamp is not greater than the stored pastBlockTime, pastBlockTime remains unchanged); the mutant that removed the timestamp guard can update pastBlockTime even when block.timestamp is not greater, violating this rule for some inputs.

After any payable fallback call with exactly 10 ether, the reference contract only advances pastBlockTime when block.timestamp is strictly greater than its prior value; the mutant (which removes that guard) can update pastBlockTime even when block.timestamp is not greater, violating this invariant for some inputs.

For any caller sending exactly 10 ether to C.fallback, the correct contract only updates pastBlockTime when the current block.timestamp is strictly greater than the stored pastBlockTime; the mutant (which removes that guard) can update pastBlockTime even when block.timestamp is not greater, so there exist inputs (block.timestamp and call ordering) that make the mutant's stored pastBlockTime differ from the original.

For all calls sending exactly 10 ether to fallback, C only updates pastBlockTime when block.timestamp strictly increases relative to its stored value; removing that guard allows updating pastBlockTime even when timestamp has not advanced, so there exist block.timestamp / ordering inputs that make the mutant change pastBlockTime while the reference does not.

For any call that sends exactly 10 ether to C.fallback, the original contract never updates pastBlockTime when block.timestamp is less-than-or-equal to its stored pastBlockTime, whereas the mutant (which removed that require) can update pastBlockTime even when block.timestamp <= prior pastBlockTime, so there exist inputs (a specific prior pastBlockTime and a non-advancing block.timestamp) that make the mutant's pastBlockTime differ from the original.

After any successful payable call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether from any EOA at a strictly later timestamp, the contract's public pastBlockTime must equal the block.timestamp + 1 (reference); the mutant that stores block.timestamp instead will sometimes leave pastBlockTime equal to block.timestamp, breaking this invariant.

For any call to fallback that sends exactly 10 ether and occurs at a strictly later timestamp than pastBlockTime, the reference contract always sets pastBlockTime to block.timestamp + 1 after the call; the mutant sets pastBlockTime to block.timestamp for some inputs, violating that rule.

For any caller sending exactly 10 ether when block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, the reference contract always retains its balance unless the block.number is divisible by 15; the mutant unconditionally forwards balance, so there exist inputs (block numbers not divisible by 15) where the mutant causes address(c).balance to become zero while the reference keeps it nonzero.

For every valid call sending exactly 10 ether when block.timestamp > pastBlockTime, the reference contract preserves some positive contract balance after the fallback (unless block.number % 15 == 0) — equivalently: there exists at least one admissible input (a block.number not divisible by 15 with the other preconditions) where the mutant drains the balance but the reference does not; the rule: when block.number % 15 != 0 and caller sends 10 ether with timestamp > pastBlockTime, the reference leaves address(c).balance >= 10 ether while the mutant leaves it == 0.

Whenever fallback is invoked with exactly 10 ether and block.number % 15 == 0, the reference contract sends its entire balance out to the caller (so address(c).balance == 0 after the call); the mutant that transfers to address(this) keeps the balance > 0, violating this property for some inputs.

For any caller and any admissible timestamp/block conditions, when fallback is invoked with exactly 10 ether at a block where block.number % 15 == 0 the reference contract forwards its entire balance to the caller (leaving address(c).balance == 0), whereas the mutant that transfers to address(this) preserves the balance > 0; the test asserts address(c).balance == 0 after such a call (fuzzing the caller and using a helper callee to accept the transfer).

Whenever fallback is invoked with msg.value == 10 ether at a block where block.number % 15 == 0, the reference contract forwards its entire balance out to the caller (leaving address(c).balance == 0); the mutant that transfers to address(this) keeps the balance > 0, so the property 'address(c).balance == 0 after such a call' holds for the reference for all admissible inputs and is violated by the mutant for some inputs.
